aplomb

uh-PLOM · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Aplomb is self-confidence or poise, especially when things go wrong.

The intern handled the surprise visit from the company's largest client with such aplomb that no one guessed she had started the job only that morning.

Worked Example

The figure skater fell hard midway through her routine but rose immediately, finished the program with a smile, and even added an extra flourish at the end -- all with such aplomb that the judges gave her bonus points for composure.

Recovering instantly and finishing smoothly, without visible panic or embarrassment, is exactly what aplomb describes: steady self-possession, especially right after something goes wrong.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

composure: Composure is the everyday state of being calm and in control of yourself, and it is something you can lose and quietly get back. Aplomb is composure with flair: confident, impressive steadiness shown exactly when something goes wrong, and it always sounds like praise.

poise: Poise is graceful, balanced self-control — the steady, elegant bearing of a dancer or a practiced speaker. Aplomb shifts the accent from grace to confidence under fire: poise describes how smoothly you carry yourself, while aplomb is earned the moment a surprise or setback tests that smoothness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

nervousness: an anxious, jittery lack of confidence

panic: a sudden loss of control from fear or shock

Where it sits · how steady it stays under pressure — confidence → aplomb → equanimity

confidence vs. aplomb: Confidence is weaker than aplomb on this scale: a confident speaker believes she will do well, but only aplomb tells you she actually stayed smooth and self-possessed when the microphone died mid-speech.

equanimity vs. aplomb: Equanimity is stronger than aplomb here: aplomb is confident composure in one rough moment, while equanimity is a deep, settled evenness that stays undisturbed through weeks of bad news.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — a-

prefix — a-: according to (French)

root — plomb (plumbum)

root — plomb (plumbum): lead (the metal) (French, from Latin plumbum)

Put it together

Put it together: Aplomb comes from French a plomb, 'according to the plumb line' -- a- ('according to') plus plomb ('lead,' Latin plumbum), the weighted cord builders hang to check that a wall stands perfectly straight. Someone with aplomb stays exactly that steady and upright, even when things go wrong.

Use the root in a new word: plumber

Word Choice

Aplomb is a warmly admiring word -- it's almost always used as a compliment for someone who stays impressively composed under pressure, not just for ordinary calm.
